LEARNING PATH LESSON · FACES & VISUAL TRACKING · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

Happy face — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

Somewhere in these weeks many babies aim their first real smile at a face — this lesson shows you how to invite one with the happy face card, without ever demanding it.

What is this?

A happy face is a face with the mouth turned up. Babies meet smiles three ways at this age: the drawn one on the card, the ones you wear, and the brand-new ones they make themselves — social smiles aimed at people, not at wind or sleep.

What does it mean?

Between six and twelve weeks smiling stops being reflex and starts being social: your baby sees a face, feels good, and the mouth joins in. A bold high-contrast smile is easy to find and easy to imitate, which is why face cards have a reputation for pulling grins out.

What does the child need to know?

The three smiles worth telling apart: reflex (arrives in sleep, gone in a flash), wind (mid-feed, grimace-shaped), social (aimed at you or the card, slower, with bright eyes). Only the third is conversation, and it cannot be commanded — only invited.

Why this matters

A social smile is your baby’s first tool for holding an adult’s attention, and it works both ways: smiling releases the good feeling that makes looking, cooing and turn-taking worth repeating. It is the opening move of friendship.

What it teaches

Social-emotional bonding, facial imitation (the forerunner of all copying), visual discrimination of expressions, and turn-taking — smile, reply, smile again.

Words to learn

smilehappyhellofaceagainmy turn

Say this to your child

“"Happy face! Look at that big smile. I have a smile too — see? Can you find my smile? There it is. Hello, happy baby. Smiles go back and forth, all day long."”

Step by step

  1. Pick an alert, fed, changed moment and show the card at focusing distance, smile-side up, where the light falls on it.
  2. Say its name slowly and warmly: "Happy face. What a big smile." Then simply let your baby look.
  3. Copy the card — hold the same wide smile on your own face and keep it there, so card and parent match.
  4. Watch the mouth corners. Any upward twitch, soft open-mouth look or full grin gets a delighted reply from you, out loud.
  5. End the moment while it is still sweet — one good smile, named and answered, is the whole class for the day.

Look closer at the picture

The artwork is a bold high-contrast smiley face — wide upturned mouth, simple open features, nothing busy behind it. Say what you see, then turn the noticing outward: which expression is your baby wearing right now?

Ask your child

Watch for the reply chain: does your smile earn one back? Does the card hold attention longer on some days than others? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if that smile was for me or for the card — I will try again after lunch."

What your child can say or do

You might get a full gummy grin aimed at the card, a slower sleepy smile for you, a kick of the legs, a coo, or a long studying stare with the smile arriving only when you copy the face — every version is a pass.

Out in the real world

Smiles travel through the whole day: the one that greets a sibling, the one that lands on grandma on a video call, the one your baby practises on the changing mat. Each one proves the card’s lesson — faces answer faces.

Try it together

Copy-cat faces: make three slow expressions — smile, wide-open surprise, tongue out — pausing ten seconds between each. You are not teaching expressions yet; you are showing your baby that faces are a game two people can play.

Understanding check

Quick parent self-check: did you spot one social smile today, and did you answer it out loud within a second or two? Answering promptly is the half of the skill that belongs to you.

Parent tips

Do not work for a smile — leaning in with a strained grin teaches effort, not warmth. A tired or overloaded baby may stare blankly; that is a no for now, not a no forever. Both parents, and any siblings, can run this lesson — more faces, more practice.

Staying safe

Hold the card yourself at all times and keep it out of the cot — a newborn cannot push a card off their face. If your baby turns away, arches or cries, end the session; fussing is how this age says the show is over.

This lesson pairs with the Happy face flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Faces & Visual Tracking (Newborn 2).
